questions.q: Which red cell picture is characteristic of iron deficiency anemia?
ch: Microcytic, hypochromic red cells with a low MCV and a low MCH
Normocytic red cells with brisk reticulocytosis and a low haptoglobin
Normocytic cells with sickle forms and Howell-Jolly bodies
Macrocytic oval cells with a high reticulocyte count
Macrocytic cells with hypersegmented neutrophils on the smear
questions.exp: Insufficient iron for heme synthesis starves hemoglobin production, so the red cells are microcytic (low MCV) and hypochromic (low MCH) with reduced hemoglobin content, usually with a high RDW.
why: Normocytic anemia with reticulocytosis points to hemolysis rather than iron-starved erythropoiesis.
Sickle forms and Howell-Jolly bodies belong to sickle cell disease with functional asplenia.
Iron deficiency lowers the MCV; oval macrocytes with a high reticulocyte count are not its pattern.
Macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils is the megaloblastic picture of B12 or folate deficiency.

questions.q: A woman with menorrhagia reports pagophagia — a craving for chewing ice. Which additional classic clue supports iron deficiency?
ch: Gum infiltration with petechiae and easy bruising
Koilonychia (spoon nails) with angular cheilitis and glossitis
Hypersegmented neutrophils with loss of vibration sense
Scleral icterus with splenomegaly and dark urine
Painless lymphadenopathy with drenching night sweats
questions.exp: Pica and ice craving (pagophagia) are classic and surprisingly specific clues to iron deficiency that resolve quickly with iron; other classic signs are koilonychia (spoon nails), angular cheilitis, and glossitis.
why: Gum infiltration with petechiae suggests leukemic marrow infiltration rather than iron deficiency.
Hypersegmented neutrophils and lost vibration sense indicate B12 deficiency, not depleted iron stores.
Icterus, splenomegaly, and dark urine suggest hemolysis rather than iron deficiency.
Painless nodes with night sweats describe lymphoma, not an iron-deficient state.

questions.q: Which single laboratory test is the most useful confirmatory test for iron deficiency?
ch: Mean corpuscular volume reported by the automated CBC analyzer
Red cell distribution width reported with the routine CBC indices
Reticulocyte count obtained before any iron therapy is started
Serum ferritin, with a value under 30 ng/mL considered diagnostic
Total iron binding capacity measured on a fasting blood sample
questions.exp: Low serum ferritin is the single best test for iron deficiency — under 30 ng/mL is diagnostic and under 15 is highly specific — though it is an acute-phase reactant that can be falsely normal in infection or inflammation.
why: A low MCV identifies a microcytic anemia but cannot separate iron deficiency from thalassemia or the other TAILS causes.
A high RDW favors iron deficiency over thalassemia trait but does not confirm depleted stores.
The reticulocyte count tracks the response to iron therapy rather than confirming the diagnosis.
TIBC is high in iron deficiency and is useful, but it is not the single best confirmatory test.

questions.q: Which set of iron studies fits iron deficiency anemia?
ch: Normal serum iron, normal TIBC, normal ferritin, high transferrin saturation
Low serum iron, normal TIBC, normal ferritin, normal transferrin saturation
Low serum iron, low TIBC, high ferritin, normal transferrin saturation
High serum iron, low TIBC, high ferritin, high transferrin saturation
Low serum iron, high TIBC, low ferritin, transferrin saturation under 20%
questions.exp: Iron deficiency shows a low serum iron with a high TIBC/transferrin, a low ferritin, a transferrin saturation under 20%, and an elevated soluble transferrin receptor.
why: Entirely normal iron studies with a low MCV would suggest thalassemia rather than iron deficiency.
A normal ferritin with a normal TIBC argues against depleted iron stores.
Low serum iron with a low TIBC and high ferritin is the anemia of chronic disease pattern, where hepcidin sequesters iron.
High serum iron with high saturation and high ferritin suggests iron overload, the opposite of depleted stores.

questions.q: Both iron deficiency anemia and anemia of chronic disease show a low serum iron. Which pair of results separates them?
ch: Transferrin saturation alone — it is under 20% in iron deficiency and entirely normal in chronic disease
Ferritin and TIBC — iron deficiency shows low ferritin with high TIBC, chronic disease normal/high ferritin with low TIBC
MCV and MCH — anemia of chronic disease is the microcytic, hypochromic one and iron deficiency is normocytic
Hemoglobin and hematocrit — the anemia of chronic disease is consistently far more severe than iron deficiency
Reticulocyte count and LDH — both are markedly elevated in iron deficiency and normal in chronic disease
questions.exp: Both have a low serum iron, but iron deficiency has a low ferritin with a high TIBC, while anemia of chronic disease has a normal or high ferritin with a low TIBC because hepcidin sequesters iron.
why: Transferrin saturation is low in both conditions, so on its own it cannot separate them.
Both can be microcytic, so the MCV and MCH do not separate iron deficiency from anemia of chronic disease.
The severity of the hemoglobin drop does not distinguish the two conditions.
Reticulocytes are not elevated in untreated iron deficiency; reticulocytosis appears about a week after iron is started.

questions.q: Which combination best argues for thalassemia rather than iron deficiency in a microcytic patient?
ch: A high RDW with a low ferritin and a high total iron binding capacity
A Mentzer index over 13 with pencil cells seen on the peripheral smear
A low transferrin saturation with an elevated soluble transferrin receptor
Koilonychia and pagophagia together with a low MCH on the CBC
A Mentzer index under 13 with a normal RDW and normal iron studies
questions.exp: Thalassemia gives a low MCV disproportionate to a mild anemia, a normal or high RBC count, normal iron studies, and a usually normal RDW; the Mentzer index (MCV divided by RBC) under 13 suggests thalassemia.
why: A high RDW with a low ferritin and a high TIBC is the iron deficiency pattern, not thalassemia.
A Mentzer index over 13 and pencil cells both point toward iron deficiency.
Low saturation with a high soluble transferrin receptor reflects iron-restricted erythropoiesis in iron deficiency.
Koilonychia and pagophagia are classic iron deficiency signs, not features of thalassemia trait.

questions.q: What is the correct teaching for a patient starting oral ferrous sulfate?
ch: Stop it immediately if the stools turn dark, since that signals GI bleeding
Take it with milk or an antacid to reduce the stomach upset
Take it on an empty stomach with vitamin C or juice and expect black stools
Take it with tea or coffee so the tannins slow absorption and reduce nausea
Take it together with a proton pump inhibitor to protect the gastric mucosa
questions.exp: Oral iron is best absorbed on an empty stomach with vitamin C or juice, separated by at least 2 hours from dairy, antacids, and caffeine; black or dark stools are expected and harmless.
why: Black or dark stools are an expected, harmless effect of oral iron and are not a reason to stop.
Calcium in dairy and antacids blunt absorption and should be separated from the iron dose by at least 2 hours.
Tannins in tea and coffee impair iron absorption, so they should be spaced away from the dose.
PPIs raise gastric pH and blunt iron absorption; they should be separated from the dose, not taken with it.

questions.q: Why is alternate-day or single daily oral iron now preferred over multiple daily doses?
ch: It lowers hepcidin spikes and improves fractional iron absorption and tolerance
It prevents the black stools that make many patients stop the medication
It removes the need to look for an underlying source of blood loss
It corrects the hemoglobin faster than any intravenous iron preparation
It allows a much larger total dose of elemental iron each week
questions.exp: Hepcidin blocks iron absorption and release, and frequent dosing spikes it; alternate-day or single daily dosing minimizes those spikes and improves both fractional absorption and GI tolerance.
why: Dark stools occur on any oral iron schedule and are harmless, so they are not the reason for the change.
The source of blood loss must still be found — in adults, occult GI malignancy is the priority.
IV iron repletes stores faster; alternate-day oral dosing is about absorption efficiency, not speed.
Alternate-day dosing does not raise the weekly dose; the benefit is better absorption of each dose.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man has a new microcytic anemia with a ferritin of 8 ng/mL and no obvious bleeding. Beyond starting iron, what is the priority next step?
ch: Start a proton pump inhibitor for presumed gastritis and reassess
Order hemoglobin electrophoresis to exclude thalassemia trait
Arrange bidirectional endoscopy — both EGD and colonoscopy
Transfuse packed red cells to correct the anemia quickly
Repeat the ferritin in three months to confirm the downward trend
questions.exp: New iron deficiency in a man or postmenopausal woman is occult GI blood loss — colon cancer until proven otherwise — so unexplained cases warrant bidirectional endoscopy to find the source; treating the number without finding the cause misses malignancy.
why: A PPI raises gastric pH and blunts iron absorption, and it does not evaluate for a bleeding source.
Thalassemia has normal iron studies, and a ferritin of 8 already establishes iron deficiency.
Transfusion treats symptoms rather than iron stores and is reserved for instability or severe symptomatic anemia.
Delaying the search for a source risks missing a colorectal malignancy, and the ferritin is already diagnostic.

questions.q: Which complication should be monitored after repeated intravenous iron infusions?
ch: Hypercalcemia from mobilization of skeletal calcium stores
Hypoglycemia in the hours following each infusion
Hypernatremia from the sodium load of the diluent
Hypophosphatemia, particularly with ferric carboxymaltose
Hyperkalemia requiring cardiac monitoring during the infusion
questions.exp: IV iron requires monitoring for infusion reactions, and ferric carboxymaltose in particular is associated with hypophosphatemia; modern formulations rarely cause anaphylaxis.
why: Hypercalcemia is not associated with ferric carboxymaltose or other IV iron products.
Hypoglycemia is not a monitored complication of iron repletion.
Hypernatremia is not linked to the iron preparations used for repletion.
Hyperkalemia is not a recognized effect of intravenous iron infusion.

questions.q: Which blood picture defines the megaloblastic anemia of B12 or folate deficiency?
ch: Microcytic hypochromic cells with a high RDW and pencil cells
Macrocytic anemia with an MCV over 100 and hypersegmented neutrophils
Normocytic anemia with sickle cells and target cells on the smear
Normocytic anemia with circulating blasts and Auer rods
Macrocytic anemia with a high reticulocyte count and normal neutrophils
questions.exp: Deficiency of B12 or folate stalls nuclear maturation while the cytoplasm keeps growing, producing a macrocytic anemia with an MCV over 100, oval macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils, and low reticulocytes.
why: Microcytic hypochromic cells with pencil cells describe iron deficiency, not a megaloblastic process.
Sickle cells and target cells belong to sickle cell disease rather than vitamin deficiency.
Blasts and Auer rods indicate acute myeloid leukemia rather than megaloblastic anemia.
Reticulocytes are low because erythropoiesis is ineffective; reticulocytosis is a non-megaloblastic cause of macrocytosis.

questions.q: Which statement comparing B12 and folate deficiency is correct?
ch: Both deficiencies raise methylmalonic acid to about the same degree
Folate stores last years while B12 stores deplete within months
Only folate deficiency produces a macrocytic anemia with MCV over 100
Only folate deficiency produces hypersegmented neutrophils on the smear
Only B12 deficiency causes neurologic disease from demyelination
questions.exp: Both deficiencies cause a macrocytic megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, but only B12 deficiency causes neurologic disease — demyelination of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.
why: MMA rises only in B12 deficiency and stays normal in folate deficiency.
It is the reverse: B12 stores last years while folate stores deplete in months.
Both deficiencies produce macrocytosis with an MCV over 100.
Hypersegmented neutrophils occur in both B12 and folate deficiency.

questions.q: Which peripheral smear finding is the earliest and most specific sign of megaloblastic anemia?
ch: Hypersegmented neutrophils with five or more nuclear lobes
Howell-Jolly bodies within the circulating red cells
Smudge cells against a background lymphocytosis
Pencil cells with an elevated platelet count
Fragmented red cells with marked polychromasia
questions.exp: Hypersegmented neutrophils with five or more lobes are the earliest and most specific smear finding in megaloblastic anemia, appearing alongside oval macrocytes.
why: Howell-Jolly bodies signal functional asplenia, as in sickle cell disease.
Smudge cells with a lymphocytosis point to chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
Pencil cells with thrombocytosis are seen in iron deficiency anemia.
Fragmented red cells indicate mechanical destruction, not a megaloblastic marrow.

questions.q: A patient has a borderline serum B12 level. Which pattern confirms B12 deficiency rather than folate deficiency?
ch: Methylmalonic acid normal with homocysteine elevated
Methylmalonic acid elevated with homocysteine elevated
Methylmalonic acid elevated with homocysteine normal and a low LDH
Homocysteine elevated with a normal serum folate and a normal LDH
Methylmalonic acid normal with homocysteine also normal
questions.exp: B12 runs the methylmalonyl-CoA reaction, so methylmalonic acid rises only in B12 deficiency while homocysteine is elevated in both; MMA and homocysteine both high means B12, and a high homocysteine with a normal MMA means folate.
why: An elevated homocysteine with a normal MMA is the folate deficiency pattern.
Homocysteine is elevated in B12 deficiency, and LDH rises rather than falls with ineffective erythropoiesis.
Homocysteine alone cannot separate the two, because it is elevated in both deficiencies.
Both values normal argues against either deficiency.

questions.q: Why should folate never be given alone when B12 status is unproven?
ch: Folate triggers a hemolytic crisis in patients with pernicious anemia
Folate blocks absorption of dietary B12 in the terminal ileum
Folate corrects the anemia while neurologic damage progresses irreversibly
Folate causes hypokalemia during the first days of therapy
Folate raises methylmalonic acid and masks the folate diagnosis
questions.exp: Giving folate alone corrects the megaloblastic anemia but does nothing for the neurologic damage of B12 deficiency, which continues and may become irreversible — a can't-miss error, so confirm B12 first.
why: Folate does not provoke hemolysis; the danger is unopposed neurologic decline.
Folate does not block B12 absorption; the danger is masking the anemia, not causing malabsorption.
Hypokalemia is a risk of brisk erythropoiesis after B12 repletion, not a reason to withhold folate.
MMA is elevated by B12 deficiency, and folate replacement does not raise it.

questions.q: Which finding best supports pernicious anemia as the cause of a patient's B12 deficiency?
ch: A history of long-term metformin therapy
A strictly vegan diet for the past two years
Prior ileal resection for Crohn's disease
Chronic heavy alcohol use with poor intake
A positive anti-intrinsic factor antibody
questions.exp: Pernicious anemia is autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor; anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies support it, it is associated with other autoimmune disease and increased gastric cancer risk, and it requires lifelong B12 therapy.
why: Metformin is a common cause of B12 deficiency, but through a drug effect rather than autoimmune intrinsic factor loss.
A vegan diet causes dietary B12 deficiency, which responds to high-dose oral replacement.
Ileal disease or resection causes B12 malabsorption without autoimmune intrinsic factor loss.
Alcoholism is the classic cause of folate deficiency from poor intake.

questions.q: Which electrolyte must be watched in the first days after starting B12 for a severe megaloblastic anemia?
ch: Potassium
Phosphate
Sodium
Calcium
Magnesium
questions.exp: As the marrow ramps up and new cells consume potassium, a refeeding-like hypokalemia can develop in the first days of B12 therapy; check potassium early and report weakness or ECG changes.
why: Phosphate monitoring belongs to intravenous iron therapy, not B12 repletion.
Sodium shifts are not the recognized risk of early B12 repletion.
Calcium is not the electrolyte consumed by brisk erythropoiesis after B12.
Magnesium is not the electrolyte monitored during B12 repletion.

questions.q: Which commonly prescribed drug is an under-recognized cause of B12 deficiency?
ch: Methotrexate
Trimethoprim
Phenytoin
Metformin
Leucovorin
questions.exp: Metformin, along with proton pump inhibitors, is a common and under-recognized cause of B12 deficiency; long-term users benefit from periodic B12 screening.
why: Methotrexate is an antifolate and causes folate deficiency.
Trimethoprim impairs folate metabolism and causes folate rather than B12 deficiency.
Phenytoin is a classic drug cause of folate deficiency.
Leucovorin is given to rescue antifolate toxicity rather than to cause a deficiency.

questions.q: A patient with macrocytic anemia has a low reticulocyte count with an elevated LDH and elevated indirect bilirubin. What explains this combination?
ch: Hypersplenism trapping mature red cells in the spleen
Peripheral destruction of red cells by autoantibodies
Ineffective intramedullary hemolysis from megaloblastic erythropoiesis
Acute blood loss with a delayed marrow response
Iron overload accumulated from repeated transfusion
questions.exp: In megaloblastic anemia the marrow makes cells that die before release, so reticulocytes stay low while LDH and indirect bilirubin rise — ineffective intramedullary hemolysis rather than peripheral destruction.
why: Splenic trapping is peripheral destruction, which would raise the reticulocyte count.
Peripheral autoimmune destruction would drive the reticulocyte count up, not down.
Acute blood loss does not produce macrocytosis with a high LDH and indirect bilirubin.
Iron overload follows chronic transfusion and does not cause megaloblastic changes.

questions.q: A patient with B12 deficiency has paresthesias, impaired vibration and position sense, and an unsteady gait. Which nursing action is the priority?
ch: Start folic acid alone to correct the anemia more quickly
Restrict fluids to keep the ataxia from getting worse
Enforce bed rest until the vibration sense has normalized
Implement fall precautions and document a baseline neuro check
Withhold B12 until the neurologic workup has been completed
questions.exp: Impaired proprioception, ataxia, and an unsteady gait from B12 neuropathy make this patient a fall risk, so safety precautions and a documented baseline neuro check of vibration, position sense, and balance come first; the damage may be permanent if treatment is delayed.
why: Folate alone corrects the anemia while allowing the neurologic damage to progress.
Fluid restriction has no role in B12 deficiency and does not affect ataxia.
Bed rest is not the intervention, and vibration sense may never fully normalize.
Delaying B12 risks permanent neurologic damage, so treatment should not wait on the workup.

questions.q: Which molecular defect produces hemoglobin S in sickle cell disease?
ch: Glutamate replaced by valine at position 6 of the beta-globin chain
A promoter mutation that raises fetal hemoglobin production
A frameshift that abolishes intrinsic factor production
A reciprocal translocation creating a fusion tyrosine kinase
Deletion of an alpha-globin gene on chromosome 16
questions.exp: Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive point mutation swapping glutamate for valine at position 6 of the beta-globin chain, producing HbS; homozygous HbSS is classic sickle cell anemia.
why: Raising fetal hemoglobin is the therapeutic goal of hydroxyurea, not the causative mutation.
Loss of intrinsic factor causes pernicious anemia and B12 deficiency.
The t(9;22) fusion kinase belongs to chronic myeloid leukemia, not sickle cell disease.
Alpha-globin gene deletions cause alpha-thalassemia, not HbS.

questions.q: Which set of conditions triggers HbS polymerization and sickling?
ch: Alkalosis, generous hydration, warmth, and iron loading
Hyperoxia, low carbon dioxide, and a high dietary folate intake
High calcium, low potassium, and a high uric acid level
Excess vitamin C, supplemental oxygen therapy, and bed rest
Hypoxia, dehydration, acidosis, infection, cold, and stress
questions.exp: HbS polymerizes when deoxygenated, so hypoxia, dehydration, acidosis, infection, cold, and stress all precipitate sickling and vaso-occlusion — which is why hydration, warmth, and oxygen for hypoxia anchor crisis care.
why: Alkalosis, warmth, and good hydration reduce sickling rather than provoke it.
Hyperoxia does not trigger sickling; it is deoxygenation that drives polymerization.
These electrolyte abnormalities describe tumor lysis syndrome, not sickling triggers.
Vitamin C and rest are not triggers, and oxygen is given for hypoxia to reduce sickling.

questions.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis of sickle cell disease?
ch: Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with flow cytometry
A peripheral smear showing sickle cells and target cells
A reticulocyte count with LDH and haptoglobin levels
Hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC showing predominant HbS
Transcranial Doppler measuring cerebral blood flow velocity
questions.exp: Hemoglobin electrophoresis, or HPLC, is the confirmatory test, showing predominant HbS with absent or low HbA in HbSS; universal newborn screening detects the disease at birth.
why: Marrow biopsy with flow cytometry is a leukemia workup, not the test for a hemoglobinopathy.
The smear shows sickle cells, target cells, and Howell-Jolly bodies but does not identify the hemoglobin type.
Reticulocytes, LDH, and haptoglobin document hemolysis without confirming HbS.
Transcranial Doppler stratifies stroke risk in children and is not a diagnostic test.

questions.q: Howell-Jolly bodies on the smear of a child with sickle cell disease indicate what, and what does that require?
ch: Acute chest syndrome, requiring oxygen and antibiotics
Iron overload, requiring chelation therapy
Functional asplenia, requiring penicillin prophylaxis and vaccination
Aplastic crisis, requiring urgent exchange transfusion
Ineffective erythropoiesis, requiring folic acid replacement
questions.exp: Howell-Jolly bodies signal functional asplenia, which leaves the patient exposed to overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated organisms — hence penicillin prophylaxis, especially to age 5, plus pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib, and influenza vaccination.
why: Acute chest syndrome is a new pulmonary infiltrate with respiratory symptoms, not a smear finding.
Iron overload follows chronic transfusion and is managed with chelation; it is not signalled by Howell-Jolly bodies.
Aplastic crisis is caused by parvovirus B19 and shows a drop in reticulocytes.
Folic acid supports high red cell turnover but is unrelated to Howell-Jolly bodies.

questions.q: How does hydroxyurea reduce crisis frequency in sickle cell disease?
ch: It chelates the iron accumulated from repeated transfusion
It blocks opioid tolerance so less analgesia is needed
It increases fetal hemoglobin, diluting HbS and lowering polymerization
It binds free hemoglobin and raises the haptoglobin level
It shrinks the spleen and prevents sequestration episodes
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea raises fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which dilutes HbS and lowers polymerization, reducing crises, acute chest syndrome, and transfusion need; onset is slow over weeks to months, it is myelosuppressive, and it is teratogenic.
why: Chelation is a separate therapy for transfusional iron overload.
Hydroxyurea is disease-modifying rather than an analgesic adjunct.
Hydroxyurea does not bind hemoglobin or alter haptoglobin levels.
It does not act on the spleen, and splenic sequestration remains a risk.

questions.q: A patient in vaso-occlusive crisis develops fever, chest pain, hypoxia, and a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest X-ray. What is this and how is it treated?
ch: Splenic sequestration — transfuse and monitor the spleen size
Acute chest syndrome — give antibiotics, oxygen, and transfusion
Priapism with referred pain — arrange urologic evaluation
Pulmonary edema from overhydration — give diuretics alone
Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 — observe the reticulocytes
questions.exp: A new pulmonary infiltrate with fever, chest pain, or hypoxia is acute chest syndrome, a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease, and it is treated aggressively with antibiotics, oxygen, and transfusion.
why: Splenic sequestration causes rapid pallor with an enlarging spleen and hypotension.
Priapism is a sustained painful erection and does not produce a pulmonary infiltrate.
Overhydration can contribute, but diuretics alone do not treat a leading cause of death in this disease.
Aplastic crisis presents with a falling reticulocyte count, not a new infiltrate.

questions.q: A child with sickle cell disease arrives with a temperature of 39°C. What is the nursing priority?
ch: Start a rapid saline bolus and hold antibiotics for now
Apply cooling blankets and cold compresses to the axillae
Administer high-flow oxygen regardless of the saturation
Obtain cultures and give the ordered antibiotics immediately
Give an antipyretic and reassess the temperature in an hour
questions.exp: Fever in a functionally asplenic patient is an emergency because of the risk of overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated organisms; obtain cultures and give the ordered antibiotics quickly.
why: Fluids are part of care, but antibiotics must not be held in a febrile asplenic patient.
Cold exposure is a trigger for sickling and does nothing about the sepsis risk.
Oxygen is given for hypoxia rather than routinely, and it does not treat infection.
Waiting an hour to reassess delays antibiotics in a patient at risk of overwhelming sepsis.

questions.q: Which statement about supportive care during a vaso-occlusive crisis is correct?
ch: Cool the patient down to reduce the metabolic demand of the crisis
Withhold fluids until the reported pain score falls below four
Oxygen should be given routinely to every patient in crisis
Opioids should be minimized to avoid dependence in frequent presenters
Give oxygen only if the patient is hypoxic and avoid overhydration
questions.exp: Oxygen helps only if the patient is hypoxic — routine oxygen in a normoxic crisis offers no benefit and may suppress reticulocytes — and while IV fluids correct dehydration, overhydration risks acute chest syndrome and pulmonary edema.
why: Cold is a trigger for sickling, so the patient should be kept warm.
Dehydration drives sickling, so fluids are given rather than withheld.
Routine oxygen in a normoxic patient offers no benefit and may suppress reticulocytes.
Pain must not be undertreated; opioids are the mainstay for moderate to severe crisis pain.

questions.q: A patient with sickle cell disease has a sudden fall in hemoglobin with a reticulocyte count that has dropped rather than risen. Which crisis is this?
ch: Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19
Hyperhemolytic crisis
Splenic sequestration crisis
Acute chest syndrome
Vaso-occlusive crisis
questions.exp: Parvovirus B19 shuts down red cell production, so the hallmark of an aplastic crisis is a drop in reticulocytes alongside worsening anemia, unlike the other crisis types where reticulocytosis persists.
why: A hyperhemolytic crisis destroys red cells peripherally and drives reticulocytes up.
Splenic sequestration traps blood in an enlarging spleen with rapid pallor and hypotension.
Acute chest syndrome presents with a new infiltrate and respiratory symptoms.
Vaso-occlusive crisis causes ischemic pain without a collapse in the reticulocyte count.

questions.q: Which principle guides transfusion in sickle cell disease?
ch: Transfuse above a hemoglobin of 12 g/dL to suppress sickling fully
Avoid raising the hemoglobin much above 10 g/dL to prevent hyperviscosity
Simple transfusion is preferred over exchange for stroke and acute chest
Transfusion removes the need for hydroxyurea and folic acid
Iron overload is not a concern because hemolysis consumes the excess
questions.exp: Transfusion is used for acute chest syndrome, stroke, severe symptomatic anemia, and preoperative optimization, but hemoglobin is kept below about 10 g/dL to avoid hyperviscosity.
why: Pushing the hemoglobin that high risks hyperviscosity in a patient with sickle cells.
Exchange transfusion, not simple transfusion, is preferred for stroke and acute chest syndrome.
Hydroxyurea and folic acid remain part of chronic management regardless of transfusion.
Iron overload is a real risk of chronic transfusion and requires monitoring and chelation.

questions.q: Why do patients with acute leukemia present with anemia, bleeding, and infection all at once?
ch: Circulating blasts consume clotting factors and red cells in the periphery
The enlarging spleen sequesters all three cell lines simultaneously
Chemotherapy given before the diagnosis suppresses the marrow
Autoantibodies destroy red cells, platelets, and neutrophils at once
The malignant clone crowds the marrow, causing pancytopenia of the normal lines
questions.exp: Clonal expansion of hematopoietic precursors that fail to mature replaces healthy marrow, so the normal lines fall together: anemia causes fatigue, thrombocytopenia causes bleeding, and neutropenia causes infection.
why: Blasts do not consume peripheral cells; the problem is failed production inside the marrow.
Splenomegaly may occur, but marrow replacement is the mechanism behind the triad.
The cytopenias are present at diagnosis, before any chemotherapy has been given.
Autoimmune destruction is not the mechanism of leukemic pancytopenia.

questions.q: How is acute leukemia defined on bone marrow examination?
ch: At least 20% blasts in the marrow
Smudge cells with a mature lymphocytosis
Marrow fibrosis with tear-drop shaped red cells
Any immature white cells appearing on the peripheral smear
A white cell count above 100,000 together with organomegaly
questions.exp: Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy is confirmatory, and acute leukemia is defined by at least 20% blasts — though some defining cytogenetic or molecular lesions establish AML regardless of the blast percentage.
why: Smudge cells with a mature lymphocytosis describe chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
Marrow fibrosis is not the defining feature of acute leukemia.
Immature cells can circulate in many conditions; the definition rests on the marrow blast percentage.
A very high white cell count raises leukostasis concern but does not define acute leukemia.

questions.q: Which smear finding is paired correctly with its leukemia?
ch: Smudge cells indicate acute myeloid leukemia
Auer rods in myeloblasts indicate acute myeloid leukemia
Hypersegmented neutrophils indicate chronic myeloid leukemia
Howell-Jolly bodies indicate acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Auer rods indicate chronic lymphocytic leukemia
questions.exp: Auer rods are seen in myeloblasts and point to acute myeloid leukemia, with the sharpest examples found in acute promyelocytic leukemia.
why: Smudge cells with lymphocytosis in an older adult indicate CLL, the most common adult leukemia.
Hypersegmented neutrophils are a megaloblastic anemia finding, not a leukemia marker.
Howell-Jolly bodies indicate functional asplenia, as in sickle cell disease.
Auer rods are a myeloid finding and are not a feature of CLL.

questions.q: Which studies on the marrow sample classify and risk-stratify a newly diagnosed leukemia?
ch: Serum LDH, uric acid, and a comprehensive metabolic panel
Hemoglobin electrophoresis together with full iron studies
Chest X-ray with transcranial Doppler of the cerebral vessels
Anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibody testing
Flow cytometry, cytogenetics, and molecular or FISH testing
questions.exp: Flow cytometry (immunophenotyping), cytogenetics/karyotype, and molecular or FISH testing for BCR-ABL1, PML-RARA, FLT3, and NPM1 classify the leukemia and, with measurable residual disease, drive risk stratification and transplant decisions.
why: LDH, uric acid, and electrolytes are supporting labs that gauge tumor lysis risk, not classifiers.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis and iron studies address hemoglobinopathy and anemia, not leukemia.
Imaging does not classify leukemia; the marrow sample and its molecular testing do.
Those antibodies are part of the pernicious anemia workup.

questions.q: A patient with a markedly elevated white count is found to carry the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22). Which therapy is first-line?
ch: ATRA combined with arsenic trioxide
A tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib
Cytarabine plus an anthracycline as 7+3 induction
Intrathecal methotrexate given for CNS prophylaxis
Rituximab-based chemoimmunotherapy
questions.exp: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) creates BCR-ABL1, and tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib, dasatinib, or nilotinib are first-line for CML and Ph-positive ALL, with response tracked by BCR-ABL PCR.
why: ATRA plus arsenic is the regimen for acute promyelocytic leukemia with t(15;17).
7+3 induction is used for acute myeloid leukemia rather than BCR-ABL1 driven disease.
Intrathecal chemotherapy is CNS prophylaxis, essential in ALL, not a first-line CML therapy.
Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells and has no activity against BCR-ABL1.

questions.q: Which laboratory pattern defines tumor lysis syndrome during cytoreduction?
ch: Normal potassium, high phosphate, high calcium, high creatinine
Low potassium, low phosphate, high calcium, low uric acid
High potassium, high phosphate, low calcium, high uric acid
High potassium, low phosphate, high calcium, high uric acid
Low potassium, high phosphate, low calcium, low uric acid
questions.exp: Tumor lysis syndrome produces hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia, threatening arrhythmia and acute renal failure; prevent it with IV hydration plus allopurinol or rasburicase.
why: Potassium rises and calcium falls, so a normal potassium with a high calcium does not fit.
This is the mirror image of tumor lysis, where potassium, phosphate, and uric acid all rise.
Calcium falls in tumor lysis rather than rising, and phosphate rises rather than falling.
Potassium and uric acid rise in tumor lysis; they do not fall.

questions.q: Before giving rasburicase for tumor lysis prophylaxis, which condition must be excluded?
ch: G6PD deficiency
Hepatitis B infection
Sickle cell trait
Pernicious anemia
Transfusional iron overload
questions.exp: Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because it causes hemolysis, so screen before use; allopurinol, the alternative, needs renal dose adjustment.
why: Hepatitis B screening is required before rituximab, not before rasburicase.
Sickle cell trait is generally benign and is not a contraindication to rasburicase.
Pernicious anemia has no bearing on the safety of rasburicase.
Iron overload is a chronic transfusion complication, not a rasburicase contraindication.

questions.q: A neutropenic patient on induction chemotherapy spikes a temperature of 38.4°C. What must happen?
ch: Give G-CSF alone and recheck the count in the morning
Give an antipyretic and continue with routine monitoring
Transfuse irradiated platelets and observe overnight
Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour
Wait for the blood culture results before starting antibiotics
questions.exp: Any fever in a neutropenic patient is a medical emergency: obtain cultures and give empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour, alongside strict neutropenic precautions and hand hygiene.
why: G-CSF does not treat an established infection and delays definitive therapy.
An antipyretic masks the fever without treating a potentially fatal infection.
Platelets address bleeding risk rather than neutropenic infection.
Cultures are drawn first, but antibiotics must not wait for the results to return.

questions.q: A newly diagnosed patient has a white count over 100,000 with dyspnea, confusion, and visual changes. What is happening?
ch: Tumor lysis syndrome with hyperkalemia
CNS involvement needing intrathecal chemotherapy
Differentiation syndrome from ATRA therapy
Leukostasis from hyperleukocytosis, needing urgent cytoreduction
Disseminated intravascular coagulation from APL
questions.exp: Hyperleukocytosis with a white count often above 100,000 causes leukostasis — dyspnea, confusion, visual changes, and priapism — and it needs urgent cytoreduction or leukapheresis.
why: Tumor lysis is a metabolic emergency of cytoreduction defined by its electrolyte pattern.
CNS leukemia is diagnosed by lumbar puncture and does not explain the very high white count.
Differentiation syndrome causes fever, dyspnea, and edema during ATRA therapy for APL.
DIC in APL presents with spontaneous bleeding, prolonged coagulation times, and a low fibrinogen.

questions.q: Marrow review suggests acute promyelocytic leukemia and the patient is bleeding with a low fibrinogen. What should be done before the PML-RARA result returns?
ch: Hold all therapy until cytogenetics confirm t(15;17)
Start a tyrosine kinase inhibitor empirically
Start ATRA immediately and support with blood products
Begin intrathecal methotrexate for CNS prophylaxis
Start allopurinol alone and reassess in the morning
questions.exp: APL is an oncologic emergency because of DIC, so start ATRA on suspicion rather than waiting for confirmatory PML-RARA testing, supporting the coagulopathy with blood products and watching for differentiation syndrome.
why: Waiting for genetic confirmation costs lives, because patients die of DIC in the first hours.
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors target BCR-ABL1 in CML and Ph-positive ALL, not PML-RARA.
CNS prophylaxis is essential in ALL and does nothing for the coagulopathy of APL.
Allopurinol addresses tumor lysis risk but does nothing for the bleeding of APL.

questions.q: Which finding defines Hodgkin lymphoma?
ch: Sheets of CD20-positive large B cells effacing the node
Smudge cells with a peripheral blood lymphocytosis
At least 20% blasts on the bone marrow biopsy
Reed-Sternberg cells that are CD15-positive and CD30-positive
Starry sky histology with a very high proliferation rate
questions.exp: Hodgkin lymphoma is defined by Reed-Sternberg cells, the binucleate owl-eye cells that are CD15-positive and CD30-positive; non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the heterogeneous remainder, about 85% of cases.
why: CD20-positive sheets of large B cells describe diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
Smudge cells with a lymphocytosis point to chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
A 20% blast threshold defines acute leukemia rather than lymphoma.
Starry sky histology describes Burkitt lymphoma, a highly aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.q: Which triad makes up the B symptoms used in lymphoma staging?
ch: Splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and jaundice
Fatigue, pruritus, and painless lymphadenopathy
Fever, drenching night sweats, and over 10% weight loss
Cough, dyspnea, and pleuritic chest pain
Anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia
questions.exp: B symptoms are fever, drenching night sweats, and more than 10% weight loss; they are appended as A or B to the Lugano stage and are screened for at each nursing assessment.
why: Organomegaly and jaundice are not part of the B symptom triad.
Fatigue, pruritus, and painless nodes are common in lymphoma but are not the defined B symptoms.
Respiratory symptoms may reflect a mediastinal mass but are not part of the B symptom definition.
Cytopenias reflect marrow involvement or chemotherapy rather than the B symptom triad.

questions.q: Why is excisional lymph node biopsy required rather than fine-needle aspiration?
ch: Needle aspiration carries a higher risk of seeding tumor along the tract
Needle aspiration destroys the nodal architecture needed for classification
Needle aspiration cannot be performed on nodes above the diaphragm
Needle aspiration requires general anesthesia while excision does not
Needle aspiration cannot obtain enough cells for immunohistochemistry
questions.exp: Excisional biopsy is required because the nodal architecture is essential for classification and grading, and fine-needle aspiration destroys it; subtype and grade dictate entirely different treatments and prognoses.
why: Tract seeding is not the reason excisional biopsy is preferred in lymphoma.
Aspiration is technically possible at many nodal sites; adequacy for classification is the issue.
Anesthesia requirements are not the reason for choosing an excisional biopsy.
Cell yield is not the stated problem — the loss of architecture is.

questions.q: Which lymphoma is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma overall, and which marker does it carry?
ch: Follicular lymphoma, CD30-positive
Burkitt lymphoma, CD15-positive
Mantle cell lymphoma, CD15-positive
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, CD20-positive
Marginal zone lymphoma, CD30-positive
questions.exp: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma and is CD20-positive, which is why the CD20-directed antibody rituximab anchors first-line R-CHOP.
why: Follicular lymphoma is the most common indolent NHL, and CD30 is a Hodgkin marker.
Burkitt lymphoma is highly aggressive but not the most common, and CD15 is a Hodgkin marker.
Mantle cell lymphoma carries t(11;14) cyclin D1 and is not defined by CD15.
Marginal zone lymphoma is indolent and is not the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.q: How does the behavior of Hodgkin lymphoma differ from non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
ch: Hodgkin is usually disseminated at diagnosis while NHL stays localized
Hodgkin arises from T cells while every NHL arises from B cells
Hodgkin accounts for roughly 85% of all lymphoma diagnoses
Hodgkin is incurable while non-Hodgkin lymphoma is always curable
Hodgkin spreads contiguously node to node and has a bimodal age curve
questions.exp: Hodgkin lymphoma spreads contiguously from node to node and has a bimodal age curve, whereas non-Hodgkin lymphoma spreads unpredictably and is often disseminated at diagnosis.
why: It is the reverse: NHL is often disseminated at diagnosis while Hodgkin spreads contiguously.
NHL can arise from B cells, T cells, or NK cells, and Hodgkin is not defined as T-cell derived.
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma accounts for about 85% of cases, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
Aggressive lymphomas are potentially curable, while indolent ones are slow but often incurable.

questions.q: Which translocation is paired correctly with its lymphoma?
ch: t(9;22) BCR-ABL1 with follicular lymphoma
t(15;17) PML-RARA with mantle cell lymphoma
t(8;14) c-MYC with Burkitt lymphoma
t(14;18) BCL2 with Burkitt lymphoma
t(11;14) cyclin D1 with follicular lymphoma
questions.exp: Burkitt lymphoma carries t(8;14) involving c-MYC; it shows starry sky histology, is the fastest-doubling human tumor, and carries a high tumor lysis risk.
why: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) belongs to chronic myeloid leukemia, not follicular lymphoma.
t(15;17) PML-RARA defines acute promyelocytic leukemia, not a lymphoma.
t(14;18) BCL2 is the follicular lymphoma translocation rather than the Burkitt one.
t(11;14) cyclin D1 belongs to mantle cell lymphoma, not follicular lymphoma.

questions.q: Which toxicity pairing must be tracked during ABVD therapy?
ch: Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis and doxorubicin is cardiotoxic
Vinblastine causes pulmonary fibrosis and dacarbazine is cardiotoxic
Doxorubicin causes pulmonary fibrosis and bleomycin is cardiotoxic
Bleomycin causes peripheral neuropathy and dacarbazine is nephrotoxic
Dacarbazine causes pulmonary fibrosis and vinblastine is cardiotoxic
questions.exp: In ABVD, bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis so PFTs are monitored, while doxorubicin is cardiotoxic so cumulative dose and ejection fraction are tracked; baseline echo and PFTs are ordered before treatment.
why: Vinblastine is not the pulmonary toxin and dacarbazine is not the cardiotoxic agent in ABVD.
The pairing is reversed — bleomycin injures the lungs and doxorubicin injures the heart.
Bleomycin's signature toxicity is pulmonary rather than neuropathic.
Dacarbazine does not cause pulmonary fibrosis and vinblastine is not cardiotoxic.

questions.q: Which screening test is required before starting rituximab?
ch: Hepatitis B serology
Transcranial Doppler study
Anti-intrinsic factor antibody
Hemoglobin electrophoresis
G6PD activity assay
questions.exp: Rituximab targets CD20 and carries a risk of hepatitis B reactivation, so hepatitis B screening is required before use, along with infusion-reaction precautions.
why: Transcranial Doppler screens stroke risk in sickle cell disease, not lymphoma therapy risk.
Intrinsic factor antibodies belong to the pernicious anemia workup.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis diagnoses hemoglobinopathies, not lymphoma treatment risk.
G6PD screening is required before rasburicase rather than before rituximab.

questions.q: Which lymphoma can regress with eradication of an infection alone?
ch: Burkitt lymphoma with EBV-directed antiviral therapy
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with antiretroviral therapy
Hodgkin lymphoma with EBV-directed antiviral therapy
Mantle cell lymphoma with H. pylori eradication
Gastric MALT lymphoma with H. pylori eradication
questions.exp: Gastric MALT lymphoma is driven by H. pylori and can regress with eradication of the organism alone, which is why H. pylori sits among the infectious risk factors for lymphoma.
why: Burkitt lymphoma is EBV-associated but requires intensive chemotherapy, not antiviral therapy.
DLBCL requires R-CHOP; antiretroviral therapy alone does not treat it.
Hodgkin lymphoma is EBV-associated but is treated with ABVD, not with antivirals.
Mantle cell lymphoma is not driven by H. pylori and does not regress with eradication.

questions.q: A patient with a large mediastinal mass develops facial and neck swelling with distended veins and dyspnea. What is this?
ch: Tumor lysis syndrome with hypocalcemic tetany
Superior vena cava syndrome from the mediastinal mass
Neutropenic fever with early septic shock
Spinal cord compression from a nodal mass
Cytokine release syndrome from CAR-T therapy
questions.exp: Facial and neck swelling with distended veins and dyspnea in a patient with a mediastinal mass is superior vena cava syndrome, one of the red flags of lymphoma requiring urgent attention.
why: Tumor lysis causes hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury, and hypocalcemic tetany, not venous congestion.
Neutropenic fever is defined by a temperature above 38°C on chemotherapy, not by facial swelling.
Cord compression causes neurologic deficits rather than facial and neck swelling.
Cytokine release syndrome follows CAR-T therapy and is managed with tocilizumab and steroids.
